beats.t: The ship raced through star clouds. Far ahead, rabbit-ear sails bobbed just beyond reach.
All right. Walking backward. Yundal, start with the most recent event.
Recent? When I offered you a compatibility reading and Neo nearly grabbed me by the collar?
Not that. Something big. A day that cracked your life open.
Something big. There's the day I got the app. Three years ago, on the first day of the rainy season.
Yeoni wrote: App. Three years ago. First day of the rainy season. While they wrote, Yundal tilted his head.
Oh. What did I just say?
App. Three years ago. First day of the rainy season.
Ah, right. Thanks to your notes, my life will survive better in your notebook than in me.
His laugh sounded strangely thin. Yeoni turned the page and pressed their pen down hard.
How exactly does this birth-time rectification work?
For each event, we work out which houses the stars were passing through that day. With the right birth time, everything fits. With the wrong one, it doesn't.
Like trying keys in a lock one by one.
Exactly. And my first impression. That's the biggest key. Remember the front entrance?
First impression? Easy. Con artist.
Correct. That's what everyone says the moment they see me.
The circle beneath the glass spun. The eastern threshold flickered. Daytime hours vanished, leaving only night and dawn.
Next. Were you ever badly hurt as a child?
Hurt? Hmm. I think so.
Yundal's voice trailed off. His gloved fingers groped at the air, as though he couldn't get hold of a memory.
How strange. It's my story, but it feels like someone else's.
A low voice came from the bow. Neo spoke without turning from the starry sea.
Eleven years old. You fell from a ferry and broke your left arm. Your grandmother carried you on her back and ran ten li.
...How do you know that?
You told me on the Island of Wealth. The day you asked my birthday for the third time.
You remember all that?
When you take that much interest, how could I forget what you say?
Wow. Is that love or obsession?
Guard duty.
Yundal said nothing for a long time. Then he lowered his head. His shoulders shook once. It was impossible to tell whether he was laughing or crying.
Everyone forgets me, and of all people, Mr. Cat remembered.
I've never been good at forgetting. You'll have to find another customer support desk for complaints.
I've tried complaining to the universe. It doesn't take them.
Yeoni wrote: Eleven. Ferry. Left arm. Grandmother. Beside it, in smaller letters: Remembered by Neo.
There's one more thing. You said you were born before the rooster crowed. Your grandmother always told that story.
The circle under the glass spun again. One star slotted into the age-eleven event. Another into the first day of the rainy season. The eastern threshold narrowed.
The two hours just before dawn. Within the Hour of the Rabbit. I already knew that much. The problem is the minutes.
We need the minutes too?
That's what Blue Rabbit's contract said. The hourglass returns only if I personally state the time down to the minute. A clause added because no one was supposed to manage it.
The rabbit-ear airship was directly ahead. Moka wound a rigging rope around his paw and pulled alongside. The two ships collided with a crash.
Oh my! Unauthorized boarding means ten times the late fees!
I'll collect those fees in rabbit ears.
Paper swarmed over the airship's deck like a blizzard. Loan contracts. The signature field on each one gaped like a mouth.
Just sign for an instant starlight payout! Interest payable in memories!
The contracts tangled into a net. One sheet slapped onto Yeoni's wrist. The signature field began trying to write their name by itself.
My hand's moving on its own!
Give me your hand, my lady.
Yundal removed his glove. A black hole lay in the center of his palm. Ink streamed from the contracts into it.
The papers went blank. The signature fields closed. But the hole in Yundal's palm had widened by another handspan.
You said it grows when you use it!
The fine is ten skewers, right? Put it on Moka's tab.
Don't put it on my tab!
Moka pulled out a bundle of skewers and planted them in his charcoal tin. Acrid smoke covered the deck. Blue Rabbit sneezed.
Achoo! That's chili smoke! You're obstructing my business!
Island specialty. Makes you cry, right? That's the flavor.
The four ran through the smoke into a golden corridor inside the airship. Vault doors lined the walls. Blue Rabbit stood before the last one.
A dead end! But it won't help. Our Hour of the Rabbit customer can't state the minutes.
Article Seven. The customer, in person, in their own words, must state their birth time down to the minute. No substitutes!
He's right. I truly don't know anymore.
The edges of Yundal's face blurred again. The golden corridor's light passed him by, as though unwilling to illuminate someone who wasn't there.
(He doesn't know. No. We have all the pieces. We only have to fit them together.)
Yeoni flipped through the notebook. First day of the rainy season. Eleven, left arm. Before the rooster crowed. And first impression: con artist.
Yundal. Your grandmother said before the rooster crowed. What time did the roosters crow in your village?
What?
It's different in every village. My grandmother's rooster crowed at five thirty. So reliably she used it instead of a clock.
My grandmother too. She put the rice on when the rooster crowed. When it was cooked, the six o'clock news started.
How long did the rice take?
In an iron pot? About thirty minutes. She said I arrived before that. She laughed because I cried before the rooster did.
The stars interlocked above Yeoni's notebook instead of the glass. The rainy-season star, the age-eleven star, the before-the-rooster star. They all fit at a single point.
Then just before five thirty. Around five twenty.
The age-eleven position fits that time too. I counted.
How adorable, playing detectives! But he still has to say it himself. And he can't remember.
Yeoni held the notebook out to Yundal. Every word on that page was his story. He studied the paper for a long time.
You don't have to remember. You can read it. This is yours, Yundal. I only wrote it down.
I'm reading my own life, written by someone else.
Not just someone else. A companion.
Yundal drew a breath and read. First day of the rainy season. Ferry. Left arm. Grandmother. Rooster. His voice shook at the final line.
Five twenty in the morning. The child who cried before the rooster. That's me.
The hourglass around Blue Rabbit's neck cracked. Pale pink sand poured out. It never touched the floor, streaming through the air into Yundal's palm.
No! That's the most valuable thing I have!
The edges of Yundal's face sharpened. At last, the golden corridor's light shone on him. Moka silently gave him a thumbs-up.
Your face is clear, my lady. Or am I the one who's clear?
Both.
Then the entire airship lurched. Darkness filled the windows. The dark moon hung directly overhead.
Black hands descended from the sky, their fingers long. They passed Yeoni and reached straight for Blue Rabbit.
A hand that has lost the Hour of the Rabbit is useless. You called yourself the weakest. How honest.
C-Chairman! I still have three branches! And performance reports!
Collect him.
A black hand seized Blue Rabbit's vest. Glittering business cards crumbled between its fingers. His feet lifted from the floor.
Wait. Let go!
Yeoni moved before they could think. They grabbed Blue Rabbit's forepaw and pulled. Moka seized Yeoni around the waist.
Are you crazy? He's a loan shark!
I know! I still don't want him eaten!
Neo cut through the air with his transparent hand. Two black fingers snapped off. The vest stayed in the enemy's grasp; Blue Rabbit tumbled to the floor.
Without his vest, Blue Rabbit was smaller than expected. Just an ordinary rabbit with one folded ear.
...Dear customer. I'll make this one interest-free. Just this once.
Is that how you say thank you?
The weakest always survives longest! Closing-down sale in the next sky!
Blue Rabbit jumped into a lifeboat. A paper sign reading CLOSING DOWN fluttered at its stern. He vanished into the star clouds in an instant.
Back on their ship, Yundal sank onto the deck and opened his right hand. Pale pink sand glittered in the lines of his palm.
But the hole at its center remained. It hadn't shrunk at all. The sand circled its rim, resisting being drawn inside.
We found your hour. Why won't it close?
The hour was stolen. The hole, I dug myself. Even when the thief is gone, the hole remains.
That hole will close with me. Never before me.
The dark moon slowly receded. Silence settled over the deck. Yundal pulled his glove back on, carefully, one finger at a time.
Then I'll have to follow your journey to the very end, my lady.
Don't say that with a smile. That's a fine.
I didn't say I was fine.
